question.problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{3}}?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2},\,{u}_{3}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$, we need to find a fourth vector $x$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are three pivot columns ($1$st, $2$nd and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable. From the third and second equations, we get ${x}_{3}=-{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{2}=0$, respectively. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+0+(-{x}_{4})+{x}_{4}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{4}=1,$ we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{3}}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1.$
